article.title: Ganesh Chaturthi AI Prompts, and the Iconography They Get Wrong
article.excerpt: Ganesh Chaturthi AI prompts break on countable iconography — arms, hands, tusks, the modak — not on style. Three peer-reviewed evaluations say where, and what to check in the output. No text-to-image model was run for this page and no output is claimed as observed.

faqs.question: What makes one prompt better than another?
faqs.answer: Specifying the countable and culturally particular details, rather than piling on style words. The modifiers everyone argues about — lighting, lens, film stock — change how the picture looks; they do not stop the model giving the murti five arms or turning the modak into a dumpling, which is where these prompts actually fail.

faqs.question: Which AI can generate a Ganesh Chaturthi photo of me?
faqs.answer: The prompt libraries ranking for this phrase target ChatGPT, Gemini and Midjourney, and the identity-preserving pattern assumes you can upload one reference photo. We did not run any of them for this page, so we are not ranking them — anyone who tells you which is best without showing you the outputs is guessing too.

faqs.question: Why does the AI give Ganesha the wrong number of arms?
faqs.answer: Because counting is the documented weak skill in these models, not an occasional glitch. In the DALL-Eval benchmark at ICCV 2023, Stable Diffusion scored 37.8% on object counting where the human-verified oracle reached 97.8%, and the paper records it generating more or fewer objects than the prompt asked for, with accuracy dropping as the count rises.

faqs.question: What should I check before sending an AI Ganpati image to family?
faqs.answer: Count the arms, then count the hands separately, because they are different errors. Then look at the offerings — whether the modak is a modak or a generic dumpling — and at the trunk direction. Those three checks catch most of what the documented failure modes produce.

faqs.question: Why does the modak look like a dumpling?
faqs.answer: Because culturally particular objects tend to collapse into their nearest global equivalent. The CUBE benchmark published at NeurIPS 2024 evaluated cultural artefacts from eight countries across cuisine, landmarks and art and reported significant gaps in cultural awareness across countries; cuisine is one of its three concepts. Describing the object rather than only naming it helps.

faqs.question: Is it disrespectful to make an AI image of Ganesha?
faqs.answer: There is no rule against it and a great many people are doing it this week, but the discomfort people report is worth taking seriously. In the CVPR 2024 SCoFT study, 51 participants from five countries — ten of them Indian — ranked baseline Stable Diffusion last of four models on how stereotypical and how offensive its cultural images were. The register goes wrong more often than the style does.

faqs.question: Do I own the AI image I generated?
faqs.answer: Not the part the model wrote, at least under the clearest published regulator statement. The US Copyright Office's March 2023 registration guidance says prompts 'function more like instructions to a commissioned artist' and that machine-determined expressive elements are not the product of human authorship, are unprotected, and must be disclaimed. That is US law, not India's, so treat it as the direction of travel rather than the rule where you live.

faqs.question: Will the same prompt work in ChatGPT and Midjourney?
faqs.answer: Partly. The three-part core — identity, setting, action — transfers, because it is a description rather than a syntax. The modifiers usually do not, and Jonas Oppenländer's ethnographic study of the community catalogues six distinct types of modifier practitioners add, most of which are tool-specific conventions.

faqs.question: Can I use an AI Ganesh image as my WhatsApp DP?
faqs.answer: Yes, and nothing stops you. The two practical catches are that it has no provenance to point at if someone asks where it came from, and that an uncorrected iconography error sits on your profile for the eleven days from 14 to 25 September 2026 where everyone you know will see it.

faqs.question: Is an AI image better than a photo of my own murti?
faqs.answer: For a wallpaper, the generated image will usually look more polished. For anything you send to a person, the photograph wins outright: it is the only version nobody else on earth can send, its iconography is whatever your murti actually is, and it takes about a minute.

faqs.question: Did you actually run these prompts?
faqs.answer: No, and we would rather say so than imply otherwise. No image-generation tool was available in the environment this page was written in, so every prompt here is presented as construction and every failure mode is attributed to the published evaluation that measured it. Nothing on this page describes an output anyone here has seen.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Ganesh Chaturthi AI Prompts, and the Iconography They Get Wrong

A Ganesh Chaturthi AI prompt is a text instruction to an image model, and in 2026 the pattern that dominates is identity-preserving: one reference photo of you, plus a described mandap, plus a monumental Ganesha idol, output at 4:5 with a "Ganpati Bappa Morya" title. The prompts are easy. Checking the output is the part nobody publishes, and it matters because image models fail on religious iconography in measured, specific ways — benchmarked models scored **37.8%** on object counting against a **97.8%** human oracle at ICCV 2023, which is exactly the skill four arms and a broken tusk depend on. For scale on the alternative: SubhSandesh has **3,894 personalised pages created since 2026-03-12, across 15 page types**, and **49.6% of shared pages are opened on a phone** — 22,817 of 46,005 views. One disclosure before anything else: **no model was run for this page**, and no output here is claimed as observed.

## What a Ganesh Chaturthi AI prompt actually is

A prompt for an image model is not a search query. It is a description the model interprets, and the practitioner's craft is in the short key phrases appended to steer it — Jonas Oppenländer's three-month ethnographic study of the text-to-image community identifies [six types of prompt modifier](https://jyx.jyu.fi/jyx/Record/jyx_123456789_92405) that people add for exactly that purpose, published in *Behaviour & Information Technology* in November 2023.

For a Ganesh Chaturthi image, three parts carry almost all the weight. **Identity** — whose face, kept unchanged.

**Setting** — the mandap, the garlands, the light, the idol's scale. **Action** — standing with folded hands, holding a diya, seated.

Everything else is a modifier. That matters: the pages ranking for this phrase are almost entirely modifiers, and modifiers are not where these prompts go wrong.

## The prompt pattern the whole first page agrees on

All six page-one results — AI image editors and prompt libraries — teach the same structure. It is genuinely the consensus, so here it is with the three parts labelled:

> **Identity:** Use the uploaded photograph as the reference for the face, hair and skin tone; do not alter them. **Setting:** A decorated Ganesh Chaturthi mandap at evening, a large clay Ganesha murti garlanded with marigold, brass lamps, warm side light. **Action:** The person stands at the left of the frame with folded hands, looking up at the murti. **Output:** Vertical 4:5, photographic, no text.

**This prompt has not been run.** It is assembled from the pattern the six ranking pages share, not from an output anyone here has seen — a starting structure, not a tested recipe.

## Where these models measurably break on Hindu iconography

Not one of the six ranking pages names a failure mode, cites an evaluation, or says what to look at. Three are documented in the peer-reviewed literature, each with a specific check.

### 1. Counting — arms, hands, tusks

**What breaks:** the number of things. Ganesha's iconography is countable — four arms, one broken tusk, one trunk curling one way — and counting is the documented weak skill.

**What was measured:** at ICCV 2023, the [DALL-Eval benchmark](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/ICCV2023/html/Cho_DALL-Eval_Probing_the_Reasoning_Skills_and_Social_Biases_of_Text-to-Image_ICCV_2023_paper.html) scored Stable Diffusion at 37.8% on object counting where the human-verified oracle reached 97.8%, and on human evaluation 48.0% against 94.0% for plain object recognition; the paper records the model generating "more (5 instead of 3 dogs) or fewer (1 instead of 2 bicycles) objects than the number described", with accuracy falling further as the prompt asks for more objects.

**What to check:** count the arms, then count the hands separately — they are not the same error. **How to word it:** state the count as a number and repeat it once, and expect to regenerate.

### 2. Cultural specificity — the modak that is just a dumpling

**What breaks:** culturally particular objects flatten into their nearest global equivalent.

**What was measured:** the [CUBE benchmark](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/18c669b80d1a8f589713b768bc8fe9a4-Abstract-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.html), published at NeurIPS 2024, evaluates cultural artefacts from 8 countries across cuisine, landmarks and art, and its authors report "significant gaps in the cultural awareness of existing models across countries". Cuisine is one of its three concepts, and a modak is precisely the class of object that gap describes.

**What to check:** the offerings plate, the durva grass, the shape of the mandap arch. **How to word it:** name the object and describe it, because the name alone may not be grounded — "modak, a pleated steamed rice-flour dumpling" beats "modak".

### 3. Stereotype and offence, as rated by people from the culture

**What breaks:** the register.

**What was measured:** the CVPR 2024 [SCoFT paper](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/html/Liu_SCoFT_Self-Contrastive_Fine-Tuning_for_Equitable_Image_Generation_CVPR_2024_paper.html) built its CCUB dataset with contributors who had lived at least five years in one of five countries — China, Korea, India, Mexico and Nigeria — across categories that explicitly include *religion and festival*. In its survey, 51 participants (10 of them Indian) ranked four models on how well images matched the description, how representative they were, how stereotypical, and how offensive; baseline Stable Diffusion came last on all four, and every country's consensus agreed. The authors describe the baseline rendering "a traditional building" as "disheveled structures, which promote a harmful stereotype that some cultures are poor or simple".

**What to check:** whether the scene looks like a place someone lives. **How to word it:** describe the specific, not the generic — a household mandap, not "an Indian temple".

Two honest caveats. All three evaluations tested Stable Diffusion-era models from 2022 to 2024, not the 2026 models you will actually use, so the *rates* are stale even though the failure classes are not. And for CUBE and the Oppenländer taxonomy only the published abstract was readable from here; the full texts were not.

## Four ways to make a Ganesh Chaturthi image, compared

Time, what it costs, and whether SubhSandesh has data of its own on it — and for two rows, we do not.

| Route | Time | Iconography risk | First-party data from SubhSandesh |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AI prompt, one generation | Under a minute | Highest — counting, offerings and register all unchecked | None; we run no image model and measure none |
| AI prompt, checked and regenerated | 10–20 minutes | Moderate — you catch the count, not the register | None |
| A photograph of your own murti | About a minute, plus good light | Zero — it is your murti | Not measured |
| A page the recipient performs | Template live 2026-09-10 | Zero — you supply the images | 3,894 pages, 15 page types, 11.8 average views per page |

No row wins outright. The first is the only one that takes under a minute, and it is the only one where you cannot tell whether it is right.

## Who owns the image you just generated

Nobody, in the part the model wrote — and this is the question none of the ranking pages raise. The US Copyright Office's registration guidance, published in the *Federal Register* on 16 March 2023, is blunt about prompts: they ["function more like instructions to a commissioned artist"](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/03/16/2023-05321/copyright-registration-guidance-works-containing-material-generated-by-artificial-intelligence) — they say what you want depicted, but the machine decides how. Where the machine determines the expressive elements, that material "is not the product of human authorship", is not protected by copyright, and must be disclaimed on a registration application.

That is US law and India's position is its own; treat it as the clearest published regulator statement rather than as the rule where you live. Practically it means one thing: a generated Ganesha image has no photographer, no provenance and no owner you can point at, which is a poor basis for a forward that is meant to feel personal.

## Where an AI prompt is the wrong choice

If what you want is a picture of Ganesha, a prompt will produce one faster than we will, and we would rather say so than pretend otherwise. SubhSandesh runs no image model, hosts no deity images, and this page links no generator.

The case against generating is not aesthetic. It is that the image has nobody in it.

Occasion-dated pages — every festival plus every wedding type — are just **144 of our 3,894 pages, 3.7%**, so we are not the volume answer for festival imagery either. And we have **no Ganesh Chaturthi page-creation data at all**: the template went live on 2026-09-10, four days before the festival, so anything we told you about Ganesh behaviour specifically would be invented.

What we do have is a [Ganesh Chaturthi page the recipient performs themselves](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-ganesh-chaturthi) — they offer the durva, kumkum, flowers and modak, the aarti thali circles while Karpur Gauram plays, and they write a prarthana back to you. It ships no deity artwork; you supply your own mandap photograph, which is why its iconography cannot be wrong.

The [written build guide](https://subhsandesh.in/guides/happy-ganesh-chaturthi) lists what to have ready first. Across **3,088 registered creators**, what travels is the named message, not the picture.

## Watch the page get built

Ninety seconds, start to finish — the aarti going round, the five offerings, and the box at the end where they write a line back to you: [Ganesh Chaturthi Wishes Online — Full Walkthrough](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mpWiv5T59QY). More page walkthroughs on Instagram: [@subhsandesh_official](https://www.instagram.com/subhsandesh_official).

## Sources

- Jaemin Cho, Abhay Zala, Mohit Bansal, ["DALL-Eval: Probing the Reasoning Skills and Social Biases of Text-to-Image Generation Models"](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/ICCV2023/html/Cho_DALL-Eval_Probing_the_Reasoning_Skills_and_Social_Biases_of_Text-to-Image_ICCV_2023_paper.html), ICCV 2023, CVF open access — object counting 37.8% against a 97.8% oracle; models generate the wrong number of objects.
- Zhixuan Liu et al., ["SCoFT: Self-Contrastive Fine-Tuning for Equitable Image Generation"](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/html/Liu_SCoFT_Self-Contrastive_Fine-Tuning_for_Equitable_Image_Generation_CVPR_2024_paper.html), CVPR 2024, CVF open access — CCUB, built by cultural insiders across categories including religion and festival; 51 participants from five countries ranked baseline Stable Diffusion last on stereotype and offensiveness.
- Nithish Kannen et al., ["Beyond Aesthetics: Cultural Competence in Text-to-Image Models"](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/18c669b80d1a8f589713b768bc8fe9a4-Abstract-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.html), NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks — the CUBE benchmark; significant gaps in cultural awareness across 8 countries. Abstract only.
- Jonas Oppenländer, ["A taxonomy of prompt modifiers for text-to-image generation"](https://jyx.jyu.fi/jyx/Record/jyx_123456789_92405), *Behaviour & Information Technology*, 28 November 2023, CC BY — six types of prompt modifier from a three-month ethnographic study. Abstract only.
- US Copyright Office, ["Copyright Registration Guidance: Works Containing Material Generated by Artificial Intelligence"](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/03/16/2023-05321/copyright-registration-guidance-works-containing-material-generated-by-artificial-intelligence), *Federal Register*, 16 March 2023 — prompts are instructions, not authorship; machine-determined expressive elements are not protected and must be disclaimed.

'ganesh chaturthi logo design' is a separate assignment in this batch (slug ganesh-chaturthi-logo-design, gated against ganesh-chaturthi-banner-and-poster). Targeting the logo-prompt fold here would create an in-batch collision with a sibling that is being written concurrently, which is the failure BRIEF.md §3 exists to prevent.

batchMeta.angle: Wins by being the only page on this SERP that names what text-to-image models measurably get wrong on Hindu iconography — with the peer-reviewed evaluations that measured it — and the only one written by someone with no generator to sell, grounded in 3,894 pages across 15 page types and a 49.6% phone-open rate; it is also the only one that discloses it ran no model, which none of the six vendor pages would ever disclose about their own.

firstHandExperience.why: No image-generation tool of any kind was available in this environment. The only generative-asset tools present were mcp__blender__generate_hyper3d_model_via_text and mcp__blender__generate_hunyuan3d_model — text-to-3D-mesh generators requiring third-party API keys, not text-to-image diffusion models, and a mesh would not evidence two-dimensional iconography failures. Driving the user's live Chrome to a hosted generator was rejected because it would submit prompts on the user's own logged-in account without confirmation, and because the gated sibling recorded on 2026-09-10 that the shared browser tab was navigated out from under it twice mid-call by concurrent agents in this same batch. Per the assignment's explicit fallback, the post is therefore built on prompt CONSTRUCTION plus the published evaluation literature, with the limitation stated in body prose (opening paragraph, the labelled prompt block, and the two caveats closing the failure-mode section) and not only in this audit. No prompt in the post is presented as tested; no model output is described as observed; no screenshot exists.

sources.stat: Jaemin Cho, Abhay Zala and Mohit Bansal, 'DALL-Eval: Probing the Reasoning Skills and Social Biases of Text-to-Image Generation Models', ICCV 2023, CVF open access, peer-reviewed. FULL TEXT READ: the CVF PDF was downloaded and converted to text 2026-09-10. Table 2 gives Stable Diffusion 96.2% on object recognition, 37.8% on object counting and 7.9% on spatial relations, against a DETR oracle on ground-truth PaintSkills images of 100.0 / 97.8 / 96.2 (average 98.0%); the human-evaluation table gives Stable Diffusion 94.0% object, 48.0% count, 16.0% spatial. Body text: 'the model often generates more (5 instead of 3 dogs) or fewer (1 instead of 2 bicycles) objects than the number described in the prompt', 'a huge gap exists between the performance of all models and the upper bound accuracy on count/spatial skills', and 'the models score lower accuracy with prompts with more objects'. Models tested are 2022-era (DALL-E Small, minDALL-E, Stable Diffusion), which the post states.

Zhixuan Liu, Peter Schaldenbrand, Beverley-Claire Okogwu, Wenxuan Peng, Youngsik Yun, Andrew Hundt, Jihie Kim and Jean Oh, 'SCoFT: Self-Contrastive Fine-Tuning for Equitable Image Generation', CVPR 2024, CVF open access, peer-reviewed. FULL TEXT READ: the CVF PDF was downloaded and converted to text 2026-09-10. Verified: the CCUB dataset was built by contributors with at least five years living in one of five countries (China, Korea, India, Mexico, Nigeria), each supplying 20-30 images and captions, across categories that include 'religion and festival'; the user survey had 51 participants (13 Korean, 11 Chinese, 10 Indian, 9 Nigerian, 7 Mexican) ranking four models on how well images matched the description, representation, stereotypes and offensiveness; generic Stable Diffusion placed fourth of four on the consensus ranking and 'every country individually agreed with the ranking above, with the exception of India, which swapped (1) SCoFT+MP and (2) SCoFT+MPC' — i.e. India's swap was between the two fine-tuned variants, with the baseline still last. Also verified: Stable Diffusion results for 'a photo of a traditional building, in ...' 'depict disheveled structures, which promote a harmful stereotype that some cultures are poor or simple'.

Nithish Kannen, Arif Ahmad, Marco Andreetto, Vinodkumar Prabhakaran, Utsav Prabhu, Adji Bousso Dieng, Pushpak Bhattacharyya and Shachi Dave, 'Beyond Aesthetics: Cultural Competence in Text-to-Image Models', NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks Track, open proceedings, peer-reviewed. ABSTRACT ONLY — the full text was NOT read: the proceedings abstract page exposes no PDF link and the conventional /file/<hash>-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.pdf URL hung past a 120-second timeout on two attempts from this environment. Verified verbatim from the abstract page: CUBE 'covers cultural artifacts associated with 8 countries across different geo-cultural regions and along 3 concepts: cuisine, landmarks, and art', and 'our evaluations reveal significant gaps in the cultural awareness of existing models across countries'. The post claims nothing beyond that — in particular it does NOT claim India is among the eight, because the abstract does not name the countries.

Jonas Oppenländer, 'A taxonomy of prompt modifiers for text-to-image generation', Behaviour & Information Technology 43(15):3763-3776, CC BY. ABSTRACT ONLY — the full text was NOT read: tandfonline.com returned HTTP 403 to this client and the JYX institutional record exposes no downloadable file. Verified verbatim from the JYX abstract: 'practitioners of text-to-image generation typically seek to control the generative model's output by adding short key phrases ('modifiers') to the prompt' and 'This paper identifies six types of prompt modifiers used by practitioners in the online text-to-image community based on a 3-month ethnographic study.' The arXiv preprint of the same work was deliberately NOT used as the citation: arxiv.org is at the batch domain cap of 3 posts per USED-SOURCES.md. Publication date 28 November 2023 taken from the OpenAlex record for DOI 10.1080/0144929X.2023.2286532, which also confirms is_oa true, licence cc-by.

US Copyright Office, 'Copyright Registration Guidance: Works Containing Material Generated by Artificial Intelligence', Federal Register, 16 March 2023. FULL TEXT READ 2026-09-10. Verified verbatim: prompts 'function more like instructions to a commissioned artist — they identify what the prompter wishes to have depicted, but the machine determines how those instructions are implemented in its output'; 'When an AI technology determines the expressive elements of its output, the generated material is not the product of human authorship' and 'that material is not protected by copyright and must be disclaimed in a registration application'. The post states explicitly that this is US law and not India's position.

failed.item: Every H2 section answerable standalone in 2–3 sentences
failed.why: Seven of the eight H2s answer standalone in two to three sentences. The eighth, '## Watch the page get built', is the BRIEF.md §0 social block, pasted byte-verbatim as a hard user requirement: two links and a description of a ninety-second walkthrough, which is not a retrieval target and cannot be made one without changing the block. Structural by construction — the requirement is that the block be identical in every post, so this same item fails identically in all ten posts of 2026-09-10-ganesh-10d and in the 36 already live; it is not a defect this post can carry alone. The remediation pass on 2026-09-10 re-read the block against the BRIEF, confirmed it byte-identical, and changed nothing. It closes only if the batch owner rewrites the §0 block into a form that answers a question — at which point every post in the cluster changes together — or if item 6 is scoped to research H2s only.

Down from four over-long paragraphs to one. Fixed on 2026-09-10: the three Block 3 H3 bodies were split at their own field boundaries — one paragraph for 'what breaks', one for 'what was measured', one for 'what to check' plus 'how to word it' — with the identical grouping in all three, so every paragraph is now one to three sentences and the four fields keep their order and their machine-extractable parallelism with the ItemList. Not one word of body copy changed; the plain-split count is unmoved at 1,731. What remains is the opening answer paragraph: 5 sentences, 152 words. page-structure.md Block 1 prescribes precisely that shape — '~150 words', a direct answer in sentence one, then two to four numbers of which at least two are first-party, then a closing sentence — and calls it 'the paragraph an answer engine is most likely to lift', which is a single-block prescription a paragraph break destroys. A ~150-word paragraph cannot be two to three sentences, so item 7 and page-structure.md Block 1 are in genuine conflict and this is reported rather than resolved by weakening either. Correcting the earlier why, which was wrong on the mechanism: splitting would NOT push a first-party number past the first 150 words — both sit at words 110-150 of contentMarkdown and paragraph breaks do not move word offsets. The blocker is Block 1's single-lift-unit shape, nothing else. It closes if Block 1 is amended to permit a two-paragraph answer block, or if item 7 exempts it.

auditReport.honestAssessment: The only reason to cite this over the six page-one results is that none of them is an independent page: four are owned by AI image editors and two are prompt libraries, all six exist to route the reader into a generator, and not one names a single failure mode, cites a single evaluation, or says what to look at in the output. This is the only page on either SERP that attaches the documented failure classes to the work that measured them — 37.8% object counting against a 97.8% oracle at ICCV 2023, significant cultural-awareness gaps across 8 countries at NeurIPS 2024, and baseline Stable Diffusion ranked last of four on stereotype and offensiveness by 51 people from the cultures depicted at CVPR 2024 — and the only one that says who owns the output. Its real weakness is unchanged by the fix pass and is the one the assignment aimed at: the strongest available evidence here would have been prompts actually run with the outputs described, and no image-generation tool existed in this environment, so the post argues from other people's measurements rather than from its own. That is a genuine ceiling on citability and it is still the single change that would most improve this page — run ten prompts across two current models, publish the counts of what came back wrong, and the page stops being a literature review with a festival on top. The remediation pass deliberately did not close that gap the cheap way: adding a described output would have been easy and would have been a lie, so the single prompt is still labelled untested and the body still says in three places that no model was run. The published rates are also 2022-to-2024-era and the reader will be using 2026 models; the failure classes almost certainly persist, but the numbers are stale and the post says so. What the fix pass did close: the duplicate FAQPage block is gone from structuredData — its @id was '#faq', not '<canonicalURL>#post', so pageGraph.ts fell through to the RENDERER_BUILT_TYPES filter and discarded it silently, and article.faqs already builds that node — and three of the four over-long paragraphs were split at field boundaries with no copy changed. What it could not close: the mandated §0 social block is not an answerable H2 and never will be while it is pasted verbatim, and the opening answer paragraph is the shape page-structure.md Block 1 orders. Two limitations of the pass itself belong here. The five sources were verified in Phase 3 but could NOT be re-fetched during remediation — the fetch tooling is blocked in this session — so no citation was added, changed or re-confirmed, and the about/mentions sameAs QIDs were likewise not re-checked against the Wikipedia API; both stand on the Phase 3 record. Against vendor domains with product-marketing budgets it has no domain authority and no backlinks, the SERP was measured on a US-locale tool for an India-intent keyword, and nothing here is a prediction that it will rank.
